summary_html: **Mandatory reporters** (designated professionals) must report suspected child abuse or neglect. Federal law sets the funding and policy floor (CAPTA) and mandates reporter frameworks on federal lands/facilities (VICAA).
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — federal floor for state reporting systems  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — includes federal-facility reporter duties (recodified from former 42 U.S.C. §13031)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court held that KRS 620.030(1) imposes an individual, non-delegable duty to report suspected child abuse directly to law enforcement, the Cabinet, or a prosecutor, so a teacher's and counselor's report to their school principal neither discharged that duty nor entitled them to KRS 620.050 immunity from misdemeanor prosecution.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Kentucky Supreme Court construction of the mandatory-reporter duty in KRS 620.030(1) and confirms that the duty is individual and cannot be satisfied by telling a supervisor.
key_cases.quote: All individuals with firsthand knowledge or reasonable cause to believe that a child is abused have a mandatory duty to report the abuse.

key_cases.holding: The Court held that KRS 620.050(1) grants immunity in either of two independent situations - acting upon reasonable cause in making a report, or acting under KRS 620.030-620.050 in good faith - so a reporter's subjective good-faith belief that she was discharging the reporting duty confers immunity even if that belief was mistaken, and it reinstated summary judgment for the hospital and physician.
key_cases.relevance: This is Kentucky's leading statement of reporter immunity and sets the good-faith standard that protects mandated reporters who report in error.
key_cases.quote: a reporter may be "acting under KRS 620.030 to 620.050 in good faith" if the reporter subjectively believed he or she was discharging the duty imposed by KRS 620.030.

key_cases.case_name: A.A. ex rel. Lewis v. Shutts
key_cases.holding: The court held that KRS 620.050(1) immunity is available only to a person who acts by making a report, so a physician who did not report suspected abuse of a foster child later murdered by his foster uncle was not immune, and it reversed summary judgment because a jury could find she breached her KRS 620.030 duty to report.
key_cases.relevance: This decision fixes the outer limit of reporter immunity: a mandated reporter who stays silent is exposed to civil liability for breach of the reporting duty.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the Immunity Statute only applies to those who act by making a report

key_cases.holding: The court remanded for the trial court to determine whether KRS 620.030's mandatory reporting duty applied to a teacher, because if it did the duty is ministerial rather than discretionary and qualified official immunity would be unavailable for her failure to report a student's alleged sexual assault.
key_cases.relevance: The case supplies the immunity consequence of the reporting mandate: because the duty is absolute, it is ministerial and strips a public employee of qualified official immunity.
key_cases.quote: if the mandatory reporting laws apply, then Turner could not be afforded the protection of qualified official immunity

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for hospital staff who reported suspected physical abuse, placed a 72-hour hold on the child, and photographed and examined her without parental consent, holding they acted in subjective good faith under KRS 620.050(1) and that the KRS 620.050(14) negligence exception reaches only negligently performed diagnostics, not the decision to perform them.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion applies Peyton's good-faith standard to hospital-based mandated reporters and confirms immunity survives even where the parent disputes the abuse.
key_cases.quote: We believe the negligence exception is intended to apply only where the diagnostics are administered negligently in some way so as to cause injury to the patient

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed governmental immunity for the University of Kentucky Medical Center and held that the newborn's attending physician was immune under KRS 620.050(1) for the reporting of a mislabeled meconium drug screen that led to the infant's removal, because she acted in good faith and neither the KRS 620.050(2) Cabinet-employee exception nor the subsection (14) negligent-diagnostics exception applied.
key_cases.relevance: It is the predecessor Kentucky construction of the KRS 620.030(1) reporting duty and KRS 620.050(1) immunity on which Norton Hospitals v. Peyton and White v. Norton Healthcare both build.
key_cases.quote: having concluded that Dr. Leahy-Auer has immunity from liability under KRS 620.030(1) and KRS 620.050(1), any error which may have occurred at the trial of this action is moot

reporting_details: Kentucky is a universal mandatory reporting state — any person who knows or has reasonable cause to believe that a child is dependent, neglected, or abused must immediately report to a local law enforcement agency, the Department of Kentucky State Police, the cabinet or its designated representative, the Commonwealth's attorney, or the county attorney (Ky. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 620.030(1)).
